analysis.one_liner: Repeals offshore-account tax reporting rules used to catch undeclared foreign income.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal offshore-account reporting rules was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2013 and never received a vote or committee action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strike the 2010 offshore-account rules (commonly called FATCA) from the tax code. It would end the requirement that foreign banks withhold tax on payments to American account holders who do not report themselves, and it would end the requirement that Americans report foreign financial assets above a threshold. It would also repeal the added penalties for hiding foreign accounts and soften penalties for failing to report foreign trusts [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Americans with undeclared money in foreign accounts, and the foreign banks and offshore wealth-advisory firms that manage that money. The bill would remove the reporting requirements and penalties that make it easier for the IRS to catch undeclared foreign income [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Holders of offshore accounts and foreign banks

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the withholding requirement on payments to foreign financial institutions and other foreign entities (FATCA chapter 4) [S2] [S3].
Repeals the requirement that Americans report foreign financial assets, and the added penalties for underpaying tax on undisclosed foreign accounts [S2] [S3].
Removes reporting rules for shareholders of passive foreign investment companies and U.S. owners of foreign trusts, and caps the penalty for failing to report certain foreign trusts [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the federal Treasury would collect less from undeclared foreign income, and the burden of making up that revenue would fall on taxpayers who comply with the rules. Enforcement against hidden offshore wealth would become harder.
analysis.who_pays_short: Compliant taxpayers and the U.S. Treasury

drawbacks.text: Repealing the reporting and penalty rules would make it much harder for the IRS to detect income hidden in foreign accounts, shifting the tax load onto compliant taxpayers [S2] [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for repeal is that the offshore rules impose heavy compliance costs — foreign banks must report and withhold on American customers, and ordinary Americans living abroad have faced steep penalties over routine local accounts. This bill addressed that by repealing the rules wholesale rather than softening them, which would also remove the tools used against actual evasion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would ease real compliance burdens on banks and Americans abroad, but it would do so by dismantling the main legal tools for finding undeclared offshore money, and the cost of that would land on compliant taxpayers. A narrower fix for the expat-burden problem was available; this bill did not take it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on May 7, 2013; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no committee markup, no floor vote, nothing more in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The offshore rules this bill targeted remained in force, so banks, offshore advisers, and holders of undeclared foreign accounts gained nothing from its defeat, while the IRS kept its reporting tools. Compliant taxpayers came out ahead relative to the bill's passage, since they would have borne any lost revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Compliant taxpayers, since the bill died in committee

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; it was referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 1 Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As the committee's chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support on record; it received no vote, so no roll-call split exists [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Foreign financial institutions and cross-border banks
industries.note: The bill would lift FATCA's requirements that these banks identify American account holders and withhold tax on certain payments. Their gain (lower compliance costs) comes at the public's cost of weaker detection of undeclared foreign income.

Repealing the foreign-asset reporting rules and the penalties for undisclosed accounts would remove much of the legal risk attached to offshore structures these firms sell. The bill would make their product cheaper to use and harder for tax authorities to trace.
